title: Enhanced performance in elderly subjects following bright light treatment of sleep maintenance insomnia
authors: Patricia J. Murphy and Scott S. Campbell, 1996
research_question: Does improvement in sleep quality (specifically sleep maintenance insomnia) in elderly subjects, achieved through bright light treatment, correspond to an increase in levels of daytime cognitive functioning?

participants.description: 16 older individuals (mean age=73.1, range 60-82 y; 8 male, 8 female) with sleep maintenance insomnia, recruited from the community. 13 subjects completed the entire 4-month protocol.
participants.recruitment: Volunteered for a study to assess the efficacy of bright light for treating sleep maintenance insomnia.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Night-time bright-light exposure (BL) at 2500 lux, administered at home. Acute phase: 12 consecutive days (21:00-23:00h). Maintenance phase: 3 months, twice weekly. Active BL group (n=7) received 2500 lux at 21:00-23:00h. Control BL group (n=6) received 2500 lux at 15:00-17:00h (daytime bright light, considered 'inactive' for circadian phase changes).

Ratio of sleep time to time in bed following sleep onset, derived from polysomnography

measures.construct: Time spent awake after sleep onset
Percentage of total sleep time in each sleep stage

measures.instrument: Nadir of cosine curve fitted to continuous rectal thermistor data

mechanisms: Bright light treatment improves sleep efficiency, which in turn facilitates performance improvement.
Bright light treatment delays the circadian phase of body temperature, but this phase shift does not significantly correlate with performance improvements.
A third process (e.g., serotonin metabolism, psychological processes) affected by bright light may be responsible for both sleep and cognition changes, independently of one another.
Daytime bright-light exposure (control condition) may have 'energizing' or 'activating' effects on performance testing, even if it doesn't affect circadian phase.
moderators: Individual response to bright light treatment (sleep improvement 'responders')
implementation_implications: Alternate non-circadian treatments for sleep maintenance insomnia may also be beneficial for daytime cognitive function in the elderly.

Non-drug treatments for sleep disturbance (e.g., hot water baths, exercise, sleep restriction) are critical, especially given potential negative effects of pharmacological treatments on daytime performance in older populations.

limitations: The observed performance improvement, especially during the acute treatment phase, might be partly due to a practice effect, although several lines of evidence suggest true enhancement.
A placebo effect of bright light cannot be ruled out, particularly for the control BL group's continued improvement on some tasks during the maintenance phase.
The computer-based performance battery may not directly translate to real-world situations.

paper_metadata.title: Enhanced performance in elderly subjects following bright light treatment of sleep maintenance insomnia
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Enhanced performance in elderly subjects following bright light treatment of sleep maintenance insomnia
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Sixteen older individuals with sleep maintenance insomnia were treated with night‐time bright‐light exposure (BL) while living at home. Twelve consecutive days of acute light treatment were followed by a 3‐mo maintenance light‐treatment period. Subjects completed laboratory evaluation sessions on five separate occasions (prior to and following the acute light‐treatment period, and once per month during the maintenance period). During each laboratory session, performance levels, sleep, and core body temperature were measured. The performance battery consisted of four computerized tasks (Logical Reasoning, Stroop Congruency, Two Letter Visual Search, and Wilkinson Four‐Choice Reaction Time) and was administered every 2 h between 10.00 and 18.00 hours. Subjects improved significantly on three of the four tasks from pre‐BL to post‐BL. During the maintenance period, subjects who received active BL treatment maintained significantly higher performance levels than a control BL group. Light treatment improved sleep efficiency and delayed the phase of the body temperature rhythm. Performance improvements were significantly related only to sleep and not to circadian phase. The implications for non‐circadian treatments of sleep maintenance insomnia and cognitive functioning in the elderly are discussed.
